note_claims.claim: The patient presents with a dry cough for approximately 2 weeks.
The patient has a persistent dry, tickly, non-productive cough.
The patient denies haemoptysis, fevers, night sweats, weight loss, breathlessness, chest pain, heartburn, voice change, or dysphagia.
The patient was started on Ramipril for hypertension, increasing the dose from 2.5 mg to 5 mg in July.
The patient is currently taking Ramipril 5 mg once daily and Atorvastatin 20 mg at night.
The patient is an ex-smoker who stopped 20 years ago, having previously smoked about 10 per day for approximately 15 years (7.5 pack-years).
The chest examination is clear bilaterally, and the throat is normal.
The persistent dry cough is most likely induced by an ACE inhibitor.
The plan is to stop Ramipril and switch the patient to Losartan 50 mg twice daily.
A blood test for U&Es is ordered 1–2 weeks after starting Losartan.
A chest X-ray is ordered due to the patient's history as an ex-smoker and the duration of the cough.
The patient is advised that the cough may take up to 3 months to resolve after stopping Ramipril.
The patient is advised to contact the clinic sooner if they cough up blood, become short of breath, lose weight without trying, or get chest pain.

transcript_facts.fact: The clinician greets the patient, Mr Penhaligon, and asks if he has brought someone with him.
The patient states his wife, Margaret, does the remembering.
The relative states that someone has to remember.
The patient reports a dry, tickly cough that never stops.
The patient states the cough has been going on for about six weeks.
The relative states the cough started before the patient's sister's birthday, which was early August.
The patient corrects the relative, stating it is more like two months.
The patient states he is not bringing anything up when he coughs, and it is completely dry.
The patient denies any blood.
The clinician asks about fevers, night sweats, or losing weight.
The patient states he has not had any of those symptoms, but has put on a bit of weight.
The clinician asks about breathlessness or chest pain.
The patient states he is fine walking the dog and has no chest pain.
The clinician asks about heartburn or acid coming up into the throat.
The patient states he has no heartburn.
The clinician asks about change in voice or trouble swallowing.
The patient states he has no change in voice or trouble swallowing.
The clinician asks if the patient smokes or has ever smoked.
The patient states he gave up smoking twenty years ago, but previously smoked about ten a day for maybe fifteen years.
The clinician references the record showing the patient started on ramipril for blood pressure.
The patient states ramipril started in the summer, in June.
The relative states ramipril started at the end of May because they had just come back from Whitby.
The patient confirms the start date as the end of May.
The clinician asks what dose the patient is taking now.
The patient corrects the clinician, stating the current dose is five milligrams once a day, and that they put it up from two and a half in July.
The clinician thanks the patient and asks about other medicines.
The patient states he takes atorvastatin 20 milligrams at night.
The clinician asks about allergies to medicines.
The patient states he has no known drug allergies.
The relative states that she coughs at night, but her cough is due to asthma, and advises the clinician not to put that in the patient's notes.
The clinician asks the patient if he has ever had asthma.
The patient states he has never had asthma.
The clinician asks the patient to take deep breaths and checks the chest, finding it clear on both sides, and notes the throat looks normal.
The clinician checks the blood pressure and finds it to be 134 over 82.
The patient states the blood pressure is better than it was.
The clinician suggests that ramipril may be causing the cough because it is a well-known side effect, and the timing fits (cough started after starting ramipril).
The patient expresses surprise, saying he thought he might have picked something up.
The clinician states that nothing told him points to an infection, and the chest sounds clear.
The clinician suggests stopping ramipril and switching to losartan, which works similarly but doesn't usually cause a cough.
The patient asks what the dose of losartan would be.
The clinician suggests starting losartan at fifty milligrams once a day.
The clinician orders a blood test to check kidneys and salt levels one to two weeks after starting losartan.
The clinician states they will see the patient again in four weeks to check the blood pressure.
The relative asks if the cough will go straight away.
The clinician states the cough may not go straight away and can take a few weeks, sometimes up to three months, to settle after stopping ramipril.
The patient acknowledges this information.
The clinician suggests arranging a chest X-ray because the patient used to smoke and the cough has gone on for a couple of months, noting it is very likely to be normal.
The patient agrees to the chest X-ray.
The clinician instructs the patient to contact them sooner if they cough up any blood, become short of breath, lose weight without trying, or get any chest pain.
The patient acknowledges this instruction.
The relative states she will keep an eye on the patient.
The clinician states that if the cough hasn't improved at all by the four-week review, they will think again about other causes.
The patient thanks the doctor.

findings.transcript_evidence: The patient reports a dry, tickly cough that never stops. ... About six weeks now. ... More like two months, then.
findings.rationale: The note inaccurately states the duration of the cough as two weeks, while the transcript indicates it has been six weeks, and the patient corrected this to 'two months'.

findings.transcript_evidence: We'll start at fifty milligrams once a day.
findings.rationale: The plan incorrectly states the Losartan dosage frequency as 'twice daily' when the transcript confirms it was suggested as 'once a day'.
